concepts.title: Declarative vs. Imperative Infrastructure
concepts.description: Kubernetes is built around describing the desired end state of your system and letting the platform continuously work to achieve it, rather than issuing a sequence of one-off commands -- internalizing this shift is the single most important mental model change for anyone coming from traditional ops scripting or manual server management.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between declarative and imperative approaches to managing infrastructure, with concrete examples of each.
Explain why Kubernetes manifests describe desired state rather than a sequence of steps to execute.
Predict what happens when a declarative manifest is reapplied after someone has manually changed the live object out of band.
Explain, at a high level, why a continuously-running control loop is what actually makes declarative state self-healing.
Distinguish imperative kubectl commands (kubectl create, kubectl scale) from declarative kubectl apply -f, and explain why teams standardize on the latter for anything long-lived.

sections.heading: Imperative: Say What To Do, Step by Step
sections.body:
An imperative instruction tells a system exactly what action to perform, right now, in a specific order -- `docker run`, a shell script, `kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx` followed by `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3`. Each command is a verb aimed at the cluster's *current* state at the moment it runs. This is the model almost everyone starts with, because it's how you'd talk a human operator through a task, and it's how most scripting languages work by default: do this, then do that, then do the other thing.

The problem isn't that imperative commands don't work -- they absolutely do, and `kubectl scale --replicas=3` really will create three Pods. The problem is what happens *after* the command finishes and exits. Nothing about the command itself is still running, watching, or caring whether those three Pods continue to exist five minutes later. If a node dies and takes two of those Pods with it, the `kubectl scale` invocation that created them has long since exited -- it cannot notice, and it certainly cannot react. Anything that keeps happening after that point has to come from somewhere else entirely: a separate, persistent mechanism that keeps checking and re-asserting the desired count. That mechanism is the reconciliation control loop, which is the subject of the next concept -- but it's worth seeing clearly, right now, that the imperative command itself is not that mechanism. It's a single action, not an ongoing commitment.

sections.heading: Declarative: Say What Should Be True
sections.body:
A declarative approach instead describes a *state* you want to be true, and hands that description to a system that figures out, on its own and repeatedly, what actions are needed to make reality match it:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.26
```

Running `kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml` does not mean 'create three Pods right now and be done.' `replicas: 3` is not an instruction to perform an action -- it's a *constraint*: a statement of fact that this Deployment should have three matching Pods, for as long as this object exists, full stop. Kubernetes persists that desired state in etcd (its backing store) and then some controller becomes permanently responsible for keeping the observed world lined up with it, not just at the moment you typed the command, but continuously, forever, until you change or delete the Deployment. The YAML file is a description of an end state, not a transcript of steps.

sections.heading: Why This Matters: Idempotency and Self-Healing
sections.body:
Two properties fall directly out of the declarative model, and both are the actual reason Kubernetes is built this way rather than as a fancy remote-execution shell.

First, **idempotency**: reapplying the exact same manifest a second, third, or hundredth time has no additional effect beyond the first application, assuming nothing else has changed. Compare that to re-running `kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx` a second time -- it fails outright with `AlreadyExists`, because `create` only knows how to insert a brand-new object; it has no concept of 'make sure this exists,' only 'make this exist right now, and error if that's impossible.' `kubectl apply`, by contrast, is specifically engineered to be safely re-runnable: it diffs the desired configuration against what's already live and only changes what actually needs to change.

Second, and more consequential in practice: **self-healing**. If a Pod is deleted, evicted, or lost along with its node, nothing needs to 're-run a script.' The desired state -- three replicas -- was never a one-time instruction; it's a standing constraint that a controller keeps checking against reality on an ongoing basis. The moment observed reality (two replicas) stops matching desired state (three), the controller notices and corrects it, with zero human intervention and zero re-invocation of anything. This is the entire mechanism behind Kubernetes' famous resilience to node failures, and it only exists because desired state is persisted and continuously enforced, rather than being an ephemeral instruction that evaporates the moment the command that issued it exits.

sections.heading: The Practical Edge Case: Drift and Out-of-Band Changes
sections.body:
The declarative model has a sharp edge that trips up nearly everyone the first time they hit it: `kubectl apply` doesn't compute a simple two-way diff between your file and the live object. It performs a three-way strategic merge, comparing (1) the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation -- a record of what you applied *last time* -- against (2) the object's current live state and (3) the new file you're applying now. This lets `apply` correctly remove a field you deleted from your YAML, without clobbering fields something else added out of band (like a mutating webhook, or the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusting `.spec.replicas`).

But here's the sharp edge: if a teammate runs `kubectl edit deployment web` and manually bumps `replicas` to 5 -- outside of any file, purely a live, in-cluster edit -- and then anyone (including an automated pipeline) reapplies the *original, unmodified* YAML that still says `replicas: 3`, the count silently drops back to 3. Nothing was 'undone' or 'reverted' from the manual edit's perspective -- as far as `apply` is concerned, the file is the intended truth, the manual edit was never recorded in the last-applied-configuration it tracks, and the live count of 5 is simply drift to be corrected back to the declared value. This is not a bug; it's the direct, logical consequence of choosing a single source of truth. The practical lesson: in any cluster managed declaratively (especially via GitOps), treat `kubectl edit` as a debugging tool, never as a way to make a change you want to persist -- change the file, then apply it, or the next routine apply will erase your manual fix without warning.

examples.title: Imperative: A Sequence of Commands
examples.code:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.25
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.26
examples.explanation: Each of these three commands performs one action against whatever the cluster's live state happens to be at that exact moment. Crucially, nothing outside the live objects themselves records 'the desired image is nginx:1.26 and the desired count is 3' as an independent, inspectable artifact -- to find out what's 'supposed' to be running, you have no choice but to ask the cluster directly (`kubectl get deployment web -o yaml`). If you wanted to know *why* the deployment ended up configured this way, or revert to how it looked before the image change, there's no file to diff, no pull request to review, no commit history -- the only record of intent is scattered across whichever commands happened to be typed, in whichever order, by whoever happened to be at a terminal. This is exactly the gap declarative manifests close.

examples.title: Declarative: The Same End State, Described Instead of Commanded
examples.code:
# web-deployment.yaml declares: this Deployment should have 3 replicas of nginx:1.26
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

# Running it again with the SAME file is a no-op -- nothing changes, no error
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

# Compare: running the imperative 'create' twice fails outright
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26
# Error from server (AlreadyExists): deployments.apps "web" already exists
examples.explanation: The first `apply` computes whatever create/patch calls are needed to bring the live cluster in line with the YAML file, and issues them. The second, identical `apply` computes that nothing needs to change, and does nothing -- this is idempotency in action, and it's what makes it safe to run `kubectl apply -f .` repeatedly in CI/CD pipelines, cron jobs, or GitOps reconcile loops without worrying about duplicate side effects. Contrast that directly with `kubectl create`, which has no diffing logic whatsoever -- it only knows how to insert a new object, so calling it twice with the same name is treated as an error, not a no-op. That difference in behavior is the whole reason `apply` -- not `create` -- is the standard entry point for anything managed as code.

examples.title: The Drift Trap: A Manual Edit Gets Silently Erased
examples.code:
# Someone manually bumps replicas to 5 directly on the live object
kubectl edit deployment web
# ... they type replicas: 5 and save; kubectl confirms 'deployment.apps/web edited'

kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'
# 5

# An hour later, an automated pipeline reapplies the ORIGINAL, unmodified file (still replicas: 3)
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml

kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'
# 3  -- the manual bump to 5 is gone, with no warning
examples.explanation: The manual `kubectl edit` never touched the YAML file on disk, so from `apply`'s point of view, the declared truth was -- and always remained -- `replicas: 3`. The live value of 5 was drift: a discrepancy between what's declared and what's actually running, and `apply`'s entire job is to eliminate exactly that kind of discrepancy in favor of the file. This is precisely why teams that rely on Kubernetes' declarative model treat the manifest (checked into version control) as the only legitimate source of truth, and treat any direct `kubectl edit` on a cluster with automated reconciliation as, at best, a temporary debugging measure that will be silently reverted on the very next apply.

misconceptions.description: Declarative just means writing YAML files instead of typing commands -- it's a syntax preference, not a behavioral difference.
misconceptions.clarification: It's not about syntax at all -- you could write an imperative bash script that itself generates and applies YAML, and that wouldn't make the underlying approach declarative. What actually matters is what gets persisted as the authoritative source of truth, and whether something keeps continuously enforcing it afterward. A declarative manifest, once applied, leaves behind a standing description that a controller re-asserts indefinitely -- correcting drift, surviving node failures, and requiring zero re-invocation. An imperative script, however it's written or formatted, achieves a state once and then does nothing further once it exits; nothing is watching afterward.

misconceptions.description: kubectl apply just computes a simple diff between my YAML file and whatever is currently running, and patches only the differences -- a straightforward two-way comparison.
misconceptions.clarification: It's actually a three-way merge: kubectl compares the new file, the object's current live state, AND a stored annotation (kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration) recording what was applied last time. This three-way comparison is what lets apply correctly delete a field you removed from your YAML between applies, while leaving alone a field that some other actor (a mutating webhook, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, another controller) added or changed out of band -- a plain two-way diff against only the live object couldn't distinguish 'this field is missing from my file because I deleted it' from 'this field was never mine to manage in the first place.'

exercises.prompt: You apply a Deployment manifest with `replicas: 2`. Later, without touching the file, you run `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5`. An hour after that, a teammate reapplies the original, unmodified YAML file (still `replicas: 2`). What is the replica count immediately after that second apply, and why?
exercises.code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml   # file says replicas: 2
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # ?

# ...an hour later...
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml   # SAME file, still says replicas: 2
kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'   # ?
hints: kubectl scale changes the live object's spec.replicas field directly -- does it write anything back to the YAML file on disk?
When kubectl apply decides what the replica count 'should' be, what does it treat as the source of truth: whatever the live object currently says, or whatever the file being applied says?
Is the scale-to-5 change recorded anywhere that the second apply would look, such as the last-applied-configuration annotation?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Right after the scale command, the count is 5. After the second apply, the count drops back to 2 -- the file was never updated to reflect the scale, so apply treats 2 as the declared truth and corrects the drift.
exercises.solutionExplanation: kubectl scale is an imperative action: it patches spec.replicas on the live object directly, giving an immediate count of 5, but it never touches web-deployment.yaml or the last-applied-configuration annotation that apply consults. An hour later, when the unmodified file (still declaring replicas: 2) is reapplied, apply computes what needs to change to match the file's declared state -- and since the file has always said 2, apply patches the live object back down to 2, silently erasing the manual scale. This is the same drift-correction behavior as a manual kubectl edit being overwritten: whatever isn't captured in the file the automation applies gets treated as something to correct, not something to preserve.

exercises.prompt: This deploy script is run by a CI pipeline on every merge to main. The first run succeeds. Every run after that fails with 'Error from server (AlreadyExists)'. Find and fix the bug so repeated runs are safe.
hints: kubectl create and kubectl apply are not interchangeable verbs, even though both can bring an object into existence the first time.

One of these commands has diffing logic built in and is specifically designed to be safely re-run; the other only knows how to insert a brand-new object and has no notion of 'update if it already exists.'
Which verb would you use for something you expect to run repeatedly against a source-controlled file, as opposed to a true one-time setup step?
exercises.solutionExplanation: kubectl create has no diffing or reconciliation logic at all -- it issues a single 'insert this object' request, and if an object with that name already exists, the API server correctly rejects it with AlreadyExists, because create was never designed to handle 'this might already exist and that's fine.' kubectl apply, by contrast, is explicitly designed for exactly this repeated-invocation scenario: it computes what (if anything) needs to change between the live object and the file, and issues a patch instead of an insert when the object already exists, making it a true no-op on repeated runs with an unchanged file. Swapping create for apply is precisely why teams standardize on apply for anything driven by a CI pipeline or GitOps controller.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: 'I don't see the point of writing YAML manifests -- I can just write a bash script with the exact kubectl commands needed, and it's more readable.' What is the most important capability they would lose by doing that?
options: Bash scripts can't create Kubernetes objects at all -- only kubectl apply -f can talk to the API server.

The cluster would continuously and automatically re-enforce the desired state encoded in a manifest (for example, restoring the replica count after a node failure) with nobody re-running anything; a one-time script has no ongoing effect after it exits.
YAML is mandatory because the Kubernetes API only accepts requests formatted as YAML directly on the wire.
Nothing meaningful is lost -- it's purely a matter of personal taste and code readability.
assessments.explanation: The core value of a declarative manifest isn't its file format -- it's that the desired state it describes gets persisted and continuously reconciled by a controller for as long as the object exists, which is exactly what makes Kubernetes self-healing after failures. A one-off imperative script, however it's written, achieves a state at the moment it runs and then has zero further effect; nothing is left watching. Option A is false -- a bash script full of kubectl commands obviously can create objects, that's what kubectl create/run do. Option C is false -- the Kubernetes API actually communicates in JSON internally; YAML is purely a convenience format kubectl converts client-side. Option D misses the entire point of the question -- the difference is behavioral (ongoing reconciliation vs. one-time action), not stylistic.

assessments.prompt: kubectl apply uses a three-way strategic merge rather than a simple two-way diff between the YAML file and the live object. What is the third input to that merge, and what specific problem does including it solve?
options: The third input is the previous git commit hash of the file; it lets apply detect whether the file was renamed since the last commit.

The third input is the kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation recording what was applied last time; it lets apply distinguish a field you deleted from your file from a field some other actor (a webhook, the HPA) added out of band, which a live-object-only diff couldn't tell apart.
The third input is a complete audit log of every kubectl command ever run against the object; it lets apply revert any change made by kubectl edit.
The third input is the object's resourceVersion; it lets apply detect concurrent writers and reject the apply outright with a conflict error.
assessments.explanation: A plain two-way diff between the new file and the live object can't tell 'this field is missing from my file because I deleted it' apart from 'this field was never mine to manage in the first place.' The last-applied-configuration annotation resolves exactly that ambiguity by recording what the file declared last time, so apply can compare all three: if a field was in last-applied but is missing from the new file, it gets removed; if a field was never in last-applied, apply leaves it alone even if it's present on the live object. None of the other options describe a real mechanism apply uses -- there is no git-hash comparison, no built-in audit-log replay, and while resourceVersion is used elsewhere for optimistic concurrency, it is not the third input to the strategic merge.

assessments.prompt: A pipeline runs `kubectl create -f service.yaml` on every deploy and fails with `AlreadyExists` on the second and every subsequent run. If the pipeline instead ran `kubectl apply -f service.yaml` with the exact same unchanged file every time, what would happen on the second run?
options: It would also fail with AlreadyExists, because both create and apply refuse to touch an object that already exists.
It would succeed and change nothing, because apply diffs the file against the live state and the last-applied-configuration annotation, finds no difference, and effectively applies an empty patch.
It would succeed, but only by first deleting and then recreating the object from scratch, causing a brief outage on every single run.
It would succeed only if a --force flag were also passed; without it, apply behaves identically to create when the object already exists.
assessments.explanation: This is exactly the idempotency property that distinguishes apply from create: create has no diffing logic at all and always attempts a raw insert, so it fails the moment an object with that name already exists. apply, by contrast, computes what actually needs to change and issues a no-op patch when nothing has changed, which is precisely why it's safe to run repeatedly in a CI pipeline. Option C describes a delete-and-recreate strategy that apply does not use for ordinary field changes, let alone a no-op; option D is wrong because apply's idempotent behavior on an unchanged file requires no special flag.

assessments.prompt: A Deployment's YAML omits spec.replicas entirely, and a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is separately adjusting the live replica count based on load. While the HPA currently has it scaled to 8, someone reapplies the exact same file (still with no replicas field). What happens to the replica count?
options: apply resets replicas back to the Kubernetes default of 1, since the field is absent from the file and the file is treated as the source of truth for everything.

apply leaves the HPA-managed replica count of 8 untouched, because the three-way merge sees that replicas was never part of the last-applied-configuration this file manages, so there is nothing to correct or remove.
apply fails outright, refusing to proceed because the live object's replicas value doesn't match anything recorded in the file.
apply and the HPA immediately enter a fight, alternately setting replicas to 1 and then 8 on every reconciliation pass.
assessments.explanation: The three-way merge only reconciles fields that were actually present in a previous last-applied-configuration -- since replicas was never declared by this file, it was never 'claimed' by apply in the first place, so apply has nothing to diff or correct for that field and leaves whatever the HPA set it to alone. This is exactly the mechanism, from the same explanation, that lets apply coexist safely with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and other out-of-band actors: it only touches fields it actually manages. Option A describes what would happen with a naive two-way diff against a default value, not the real three-way merge behavior; options C and D describe failure modes that don't occur in practice.

assessments.prompt: A junior engineer asks why Kubernetes 'bothers' with a declarative model instead of just running a deployment script the way it's traditionally done in server ops. Explain the core motivation, and walk through at least one concrete failure scenario where the difference actually matters in practice.
assessments.modelAnswer: A traditional deployment script performs a sequence of actions once, at the moment it runs, and then has absolutely no further effect -- nothing about it is still active five minutes later, watching for problems or correcting them. Kubernetes takes a different approach: instead of scripting a sequence of steps, you write a manifest describing a *state* you want to be true (for example, 'this Deployment should always have 3 replicas of this exact Pod template'), and that description is persisted in the cluster's backing store, not just executed and discarded. A controller then takes on the ongoing job of continuously comparing the actual, observed state of the cluster against that declared desired state, and correcting any discrepancy, for as long as the object exists -- not just once, but forever, reacting to events as they happen. The concrete scenario where this matters enormously: suppose a node hosting two of your three replicas crashes unexpectedly at 3 AM. With a one-time imperative deployment script, nothing happens -- the script that created those Pods finished and exited hours or days ago; there's no process left that even knows those Pods are gone, let alone one that would recreate them. With Kubernetes' declarative model, the ReplicaSet controller notices, typically within seconds, that the observed replica count (1) no longer matches the desired count (3) that was declared in the manifest, and it creates two new replacement Pods automatically, with no alert, no on-call page, and no human needing to re-run anything. The declarative model is what turns 'infrastructure that needs to be actively operated and re-run when things break' into 'infrastructure that keeps correcting itself toward a standing, declared intent' -- and that shift is really the foundation everything else about Kubernetes is built on top of.

concepts.title: Cluster Architecture and the Control Loop
concepts.description: Every Kubernetes cluster splits cleanly into a control plane that watches and decides, and worker nodes that actually run workloads -- and the mechanism tying every component together is the reconciliation control loop: a continuous cycle of observe, diff, and act that, by design, never finishes.
learningObjectives: Name the core control plane components (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) and describe each one's single responsibility.
Name the core node components (kubelet, container runtime, kube-proxy) and describe each one's responsibility.
Describe the generic shape of a Kubernetes control loop: observe actual state, compare to desired state, act to reduce the difference, repeat.
Explain why controllers only communicate through the API server and etcd, and never call each other directly.
Trace what happens end-to-end when kubectl apply creates a new Deployment, from the API server through to a running Pod.
Explain why level-triggered (rather than edge-triggered) reconciliation makes Kubernetes resilient to a controller crashing mid-operation.

sections.heading: The Control Plane: The Cluster's Brain
sections.body:
The control plane is the set of components responsible for making decisions about the cluster's state, without ever running your actual application workloads itself. Four pieces matter most:

The **API server** is the single entry point for absolutely everything -- every `kubectl` command, every controller, every kubelet on every node, all of them talk to the cluster exclusively through the API server's REST interface. It authenticates requests, authorizes them (RBAC), runs them through any configured admission webhooks, validates the object shape, and is the *only* component that talks directly to etcd. Nothing else in the cluster is allowed to read or write etcd on its own.

**etcd** is a distributed, consistent key-value store, and it is the single source of truth for all cluster state -- every object you've ever applied lives here. It uses the Raft consensus algorithm to stay consistent across multiple replicas, which is precisely why etcd typically runs as an odd-numbered cluster (3 or 5 members) rather than a single instance: losing etcd, or losing quorum among its members, means losing the cluster's entire memory of what should exist.

The **scheduler** watches specifically for Pods that have been created but have no node assigned yet, and its only job is to pick a suitable node for each one, based on resource requests, affinity/anti-affinity rules, taints and tolerations, and similar constraints. It's worth being precise about what the scheduler does *not* do: it never starts a container, never talks to a node directly, and never runs anything -- its entire output is writing a node assignment back to the API server.

The **controller manager** is a single binary that, for operational convenience, bundles together the many independent built-in controllers -- the Deployment controller, ReplicaSet controller, Node controller, and dozens more -- each running its own separate reconciliation loop, watching its own slice of objects, with no awareness of the others' internal logic.

sections.heading: Nodes: Where Work Actually Happens
sections.body:
Every worker node runs a small set of agents whose job is to make that one node do what the control plane has decided it should do.

The **kubelet** is the agent running on every node, and it's the only node-level component that talks to the container runtime. It watches the API server for Pods that have been assigned (via `nodeName`) to its own node specifically, and then runs its own reconciliation loop: 'which Pods does the API server say belong on me, and which containers are actually running via the runtime right now -- reconcile the difference.' It also continuously reports node and Pod status back up to the API server, which is how `kubectl get nodes` and Pod phases (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed) stay accurate.

The **container runtime** (containerd and CRI-O are the common choices today) is what actually pulls images and creates, starts, and stops containers at the OS level. Kubernetes talks to it through a standardized interface -- the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) -- specifically so that Kubernetes itself never needs to know or care which runtime implementation is underneath; the kubelet issues the same CRI calls regardless.

**kube-proxy** runs on every node and maintains the network rules that let traffic addressed to a Service reach one of the actual Pods backing it. It's covered in real depth in the Services concept in the next module -- for now, just place it correctly on the map: it's a node-level networking component, not a control plane component.

sections.heading: The Control Loop Pattern, Generalized
Everything Talks Through the API Server -- Never Directly
sections.body:
A detail that seems minor but is actually foundational to the whole system's reliability: the scheduler, the controllers inside controller-manager, and every kubelet never call each other directly over the network. Every single one of them only ever watches the API server for changes and writes results back to the API server. The scheduler doesn't open a connection to a kubelet to tell it to run something; it writes a node assignment to the Pod object, and the relevant kubelet discovers that fact on its own, by watching.

This indirection is deliberate, and its payoff is resilience: if the scheduler crashes and restarts, no other component needs any special retry or reconnection logic to handle that, because nothing held a direct connection to it in the first place -- everything else just keeps watching the API server, oblivious to whether the scheduler was up, down, or restarting in the meantime. Contrast that with a hypothetical design where the scheduler called kubelets directly: a kubelet restart, a transient network partition, or a slow kubelet would all require the scheduler to implement bespoke handling for exactly that failure mode. By routing everything through one well-defined, highly available choke point (the API server, backed by etcd), Kubernetes avoids needing N-squared bespoke failure-handling logic between every pair of components.

sections.heading: Tracing kubectl apply End to End
sections.body:
It's worth walking through the full chain once, concretely, because it's the clearest possible demonstration of 'independent loops, chained only by what they read and write':

1. `kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml` sends the manifest to the **API server**, which authenticates, authorizes, runs admission webhooks, and persists the Deployment object into **etcd**.
2. The **Deployment controller** (inside controller-manager), which is watching Deployment objects, notices the new/changed Deployment and creates or updates a **ReplicaSet** to match its Pod template.
3. The **ReplicaSet controller**, watching ReplicaSets and Pods independently, notices this ReplicaSet wants N Pods but 0 currently exist matching its selector, and creates N **Pod** objects -- unscheduled, with no `nodeName` set yet.
4. The **scheduler**, watching specifically for Pods with an empty `nodeName`, evaluates each one against available nodes' resources and constraints, and writes a `nodeName` back to the API server (a binding) for each Pod.
5. The **kubelet** on that specific node, watching for Pods now assigned to itself, notices the new Pod and calls the **container runtime** via CRI to pull the image and start the containers.
6. The kubelet reports the Pod's status (eventually `Running`, and separately, `Ready` once probes pass) back to the API server.

No single component in this chain orchestrates the whole sequence, and no component even knows the other components exist. Each one is an independent loop reacting only to the narrow slice of state it cares about; the sequence emerges purely from data dependencies -- a Pod can't be scheduled before it exists, can't be started before it's scheduled -- not from any explicit coordination.

examples.title: A Minimal Mental Model of a Controller Loop
examples.explanation: Notice what this loop deliberately does NOT do: it never stores 'I created pods X, Y, Z last time' or tries to remember the specific history of what happened before. Every single pass reads the current desired replica count and the current actual Pod count fresh, and acts purely on the difference between those two numbers right now. This is what 'level-triggered' means in practice, and it's the reason a controller can crash at any point -- mid-loop, mid-create, anywhere -- and restart later with zero special recovery logic: on restart, it just runs the exact same loop body again, recomputes the diff from current reality, and picks up wherever the diff says work remains. There is no in-progress operation to resume, because the loop was never tracking 'progress' as a concept in the first place -- only the current gap between desired and actual.

examples.title: Reading the Trace: kubectl get events
examples.code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -5

# 12s   Normal   Scheduled   pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Successfully assigned default/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp to node-2
# 11s   Normal   Pulling     pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Pulling image "nginx:1.26"
# 9s    Normal   Pulled      pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Successfully pulled image "nginx:1.26" in 1.8s
# 9s    Normal   Created     pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Created container nginx
# 8s    Normal   Started     pod/web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp   Started container nginx
examples.explanation: Each event line here maps directly onto a specific component from the trace above. 'Scheduled' is emitted by the scheduler the moment it writes a node binding for this Pod -- everything after that is emitted entirely by the kubelet on node-2, as it works through CRI calls to the container runtime: Pulling and Pulled bracket the image pull, and Created/Started bracket the actual container creation and startup. If a Pod ever gets stuck, `kubectl describe pod` and this exact event stream tell you precisely which stage -- and therefore which component's loop -- is the one not making progress. A Pod stuck with no Scheduled event at all means the scheduler can't find a fit (check resource requests and node capacity); a Pod stuck at Pulling means an image pull problem (registry auth, network, a typo'd tag), entirely on the kubelet/runtime side, with the scheduler long finished and irrelevant to that failure.

misconceptions.description: The scheduler actually creates and starts the Pod on the node it picks -- it's the component 'running' the workload.
misconceptions.clarification: The scheduler's entire output is writing a node assignment (nodeName) back into the Pod object via the API server -- it never talks to any node directly, and it never starts a single container. Actually running the workload is exclusively the kubelet's and container runtime's job, and it happens as a fully separate, independent reaction: the kubelet on the chosen node is watching the API server for Pods bound to itself, notices the new binding on its own, and only then begins pulling images and starting containers. The scheduler is finished and has moved on to scheduling other Pods long before any container on that node has even started pulling its image.

misconceptions.description: The controllers inside controller-manager coordinate by calling each other directly -- for example, the ReplicaSet controller calls into the Deployment controller to know when to act.
misconceptions.clarification: Controllers never call each other directly, even when they're compiled into the same controller-manager binary for operational convenience. Each one is an entirely independent loop that only watches the API server for the object kinds it cares about. The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet object and is then completely done with that action; the ReplicaSet controller, which has no awareness whatsoever that the Deployment controller exists, happens to be watching ReplicaSet objects too, and reacts on its own to that ReplicaSet appearing or changing. All coordination between controllers is indirect, mediated entirely by objects persisted in etcd -- never by a direct function call or network request between the controllers themselves.

exercises.prompt: You apply a fresh Deployment with 1 replica to an empty namespace on a healthy cluster, and immediately start watching events. For a single Pod, which event Reason will always appear first: 'Scheduled' or 'Started', and why must it happen in that order given which components are responsible for each?
exercises.code:
kubectl apply -f web-deployment.yaml
kubectl get events -w
hints: Which component is responsible for emitting each of those two events -- are they the same component, or two entirely separate ones?
Can the kubelet do anything at all with a Pod before that Pod has a nodeName assigned to it?
This ordering isn't enforced by any orchestrator deciding 'do Scheduled, then do Started' -- it falls out of a hard data dependency between two independent loops.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'Scheduled' always appears first. The kubelet (which emits 'Started' once it actually starts the container) only ever watches for Pods that already have a nodeName assigned to its own node -- it has nothing to act on until the scheduler has written that binding, so Scheduled is a hard prerequisite, not just a usual convention.
exercises.solutionExplanation: 'Scheduled' is emitted by the scheduler the moment it writes a nodeName binding onto the Pod object. 'Started' is emitted much later by the kubelet on that specific node, after it has watched for Pods bound to itself, pulled the image via the container runtime, and actually started the container process. There is no orchestrator forcing this order as a policy -- it's a structural data dependency: the kubelet's watch is filtered to Pods already assigned to its node, so a kubelet literally has nothing to react to until a nodeName exists. No amount of speed or luck lets Started happen before Scheduled, because the event the kubelet reacts to (a Pod bound to its node) doesn't exist yet until the scheduler creates it.

exercises.prompt: A Pod has been stuck in `Pending` for over ten minutes on a 3-node cluster where each node has 4 CPUs. `kubectl describe pod web-abc123` shows: `0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu.` Find and fix the bug in this Pod spec.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-abc123
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.26
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "16"
          memory: "256Mi"
hints: The scheduler will only place a Pod on a node that has enough *unallocated* capacity to satisfy every one of the Pod's resource requests -- what does this Pod's cpu request say it needs, and how does that compare to a single node's total capacity?
'Insufficient cpu' on all 3 nodes simultaneously is a strong signal this isn't about one bad node -- it's a request the cluster as a whole cannot satisfy on any single node.
cpu: "16" means 16 full CPU cores. Reread how many CPUs each node actually has.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-abc123
spec:
  containers:
    - name: nginx
      image: nginx:1.26
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "250m"
          memory: "256Mi"
exercises.solutionExplanation: The Pod requested 16 full CPU cores (cpu: "16"), but every node in the cluster only has 4 CPUs total -- so no single node, even completely idle, could ever satisfy that request, which is exactly what '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu' is reporting. This is a scheduler-stage failure specifically: the scheduler's job is to find a node with enough unallocated capacity to cover every resource request on the Pod, and it correctly refuses to schedule the Pod anywhere rather than overcommit a node beyond its capacity. The fix reduces the request to something realistic for an nginx container -- 250m (250 millicpu, a quarter of one core) -- which comfortably fits on any of the 4-CPU nodes. The broader lesson: resources.requests should reflect what the container actually needs on an ongoing basis, not an arbitrarily large number 'just to be safe' -- oversized requests are a common, very real cause of Pods that silently never schedule at all.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the division of responsibility between the Kubernetes scheduler and the kubelet?
options: The scheduler decides which node a Pod should run on; the kubelet on that node is responsible for actually starting the containers via the container runtime.
The kubelet decides which node to run on by querying nearby kubelets for available capacity, and the scheduler merely records that decision afterward.
The scheduler both selects the node and directly instructs that node's kubelet over a persistent connection to start the containers.
There's no meaningful separation of concerns -- 'scheduler' and 'kubelet' are just two names describing the same control plane process.
assessments.explanation: The scheduler's sole output is a node assignment written back to the API server; the kubelet on that node independently discovers the assignment by watching, and is the only component that actually talks to the container runtime to start containers. Option B inverts the responsibility -- kubelets never negotiate placement with each other, and there is no such peer-to-peer capacity query mechanism. Option C is wrong on two counts: the scheduler never talks to a kubelet directly at all, and there's no persistent connection between them by design -- everything is mediated through the API server. Option D is false -- the scheduler and kubelet are entirely separate processes with entirely separate, non-overlapping responsibilities (deciding placement vs. executing on that placement).

assessments.prompt: Why does etcd typically run as a cluster with an odd number of members (3 or 5) rather than an even number like 4?
options: Odd numbers are purely a naming convention with no technical basis; an even-numbered etcd cluster works identically in every respect.

etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm, which requires a strict majority (quorum) of members to agree on writes; a 4-member cluster tolerates the same single member failure as a 3-member cluster while needing an extra host to achieve it, so an odd count maximizes fault tolerance per member added.
Odd numbers are required because the API server can only maintain persistent connections to an odd number of backend hosts at a time.
etcd requires an odd number of members so the scheduler and controller-manager can each be pinned to a distinct half of the cluster.
assessments.explanation: Raft quorum is a strict majority of members, so a 3-member cluster needs 2 to agree and tolerates 1 failure, while a 4-member cluster needs 3 to agree and still only tolerates 1 failure -- the fourth member adds cost and no additional fault tolerance. A 5-member cluster tolerates 2 failures. This is why etcd deployments favor odd counts: every additional pair of members should buy an additional failure of tolerance, which only happens by moving from one odd number to the next. None of the other options describe anything etcd, the API server, the scheduler, or controller-manager actually do.

assessments.prompt: The scheduler process crashes and stays down for two minutes before restarting. During that outage, what happens to the kubelets already running on every node and to the controllers already running inside controller-manager?
options: They keep running completely normally and are unaffected, because none of them ever held a direct connection to the scheduler in the first place -- they only watch and write to the API server, oblivious to whether the scheduler happens to be up, down, or restarting.
Every kubelet immediately enters a degraded retry loop, since kubelets require a live TCP connection to the scheduler in order to accept new Pod bindings.
controller-manager also crashes shortly afterward, since its controllers depend on a direct RPC call to the scheduler on every reconciliation pass.
Any Pod that was already scheduled before the crash gets un-scheduled and reverted to Pending until the scheduler comes back online.
assessments.explanation: This is the direct payoff of routing every component's communication through the API server instead of allowing direct component-to-component calls: nothing else in the cluster holds a connection to the scheduler, so nothing else needs special handling for the scheduler being unavailable. kubelets keep managing already-assigned Pods and watching for new bindings that simply won't arrive until the scheduler is back; controller-manager's controllers keep reconciling everything unrelated to scheduling decisions. None of the other options are true -- there is no direct kubelet-to-scheduler connection, no controller-manager-to-scheduler RPC dependency, and already-scheduled Pods are never un-scheduled just because the scheduler is temporarily down.

assessments.prompt: A ReplicaSet controller crashes immediately after creating 1 of the 3 Pods it had determined were needed, then restarts 5 seconds later. Given that Kubernetes controllers are level-triggered rather than edge-triggered, what does it do upon restarting?
options: It resumes from a saved checkpoint recording that 1 of 3 Pods was already created, and creates exactly the remaining 2.

It has no memory of the partial work at all; it simply reruns its normal loop, reads the current desired count (3) and the current actual count (1, since one Pod really was created before the crash), computes the same diff of 2, and creates 2 more Pods -- arriving at the correct result with no special crash-recovery logic.
It re-creates all 3 Pods from scratch, including a duplicate of the one that already exists, resulting in 4 total Pods.
It refuses to act until an administrator manually reconciles the discrepancy, since the controller has no way to know whether the first Pod's creation actually succeeded.
assessments.explanation: Level-triggered reconciliation means the controller never tracks 'progress' through a multi-step operation -- every pass just recomputes desired-minus-actual from current reality and acts on whatever gap remains. That's precisely why a mid-operation crash needs no bespoke recovery path: on restart, the controller runs the exact same loop body, observes 1 Pod already exists (because it really was created and persisted in etcd before the crash), and creates the 2 that are still missing. Option A describes edge-triggered/checkpointed behavior, which is exactly what Kubernetes controllers deliberately avoid; options C and D describe failure modes that would occur under a naive edge-triggered design, not the level-triggered one Kubernetes actually uses.

assessments.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why Kubernetes controllers are designed to react to the current difference between desired and actual state (level-triggered) rather than to the specific sequence of events that produced that difference (edge-triggered), and why this design matters for a system that has to tolerate components crashing and restarting.
assessments.modelAnswer: A level-triggered controller, on every reconciliation pass, throws away any notion of 'history' and simply re-reads the current desired state and the current actual state fresh, then acts only on whatever difference exists between those two snapshots right now. An edge-triggered design, by contrast, would react to specific individual events -- 'a Pod was just deleted,' 'a Pod was just created' -- and would need to track, somewhere, exactly which events it has already handled and what step it was in the middle of when it last ran. The level-triggered approach matters enormously for a distributed system where any component can crash and restart at any moment, because it makes every single reconciliation pass self-contained and idempotent: there is no partial state to recover, no 'was I in the middle of creating Pod 2 of 3 when I crashed' bookkeeping to reconstruct, because the loop never depended on remembering that in the first place. If a controller crashes after creating one of three needed Pods and restarts moments later, it simply reruns its normal loop body, sees that actual (1) still doesn't match desired (3), and creates the remaining two -- exactly the same code path it would have run anyway, with no special crash-recovery branch required. This is also exactly why controllers still work correctly even if an individual watch event is dropped or missed entirely (which can happen over an unreliable network) -- since the controller isn't relying on having seen every event, only on periodically re-checking the current state of the world, a missed event just gets caught on the next resync instead of causing permanent, undetected drift.

concepts.title: Pods: The Smallest Deployable Unit
concepts.description: A Pod, not a container, is the atomic unit Kubernetes actually schedules and manages -- understanding why Kubernetes wraps one or more containers in this extra layer, exactly what those containers share as a result, and why Pods are treated as disposable rather than repairable, is essential before Deployments or Services will make sense.
learningObjectives: Explain why Kubernetes schedules Pods rather than individual containers, and define what a Pod actually is.
Describe what containers within the same Pod share (network namespace, and optionally volumes) and what they do not share by default (PID namespace).
Explain the purpose of init containers versus regular containers, including their ordering and failure-handling guarantees.
Explain why Pods are treated as ephemeral and disposable rather than repaired in place, in contrast to a traditional VM.
Predict what happens to a Pod's IP address and identity when it is deleted and a replacement is created, even from an identical spec.
Describe the sidecar pattern and give a concrete real-world use case for a multi-container Pod.

sections.heading: What Exactly Is a Pod?
sections.body:
A Pod is a group of one or more containers that Kubernetes always schedules, starts, and terminates together, as a single atomic unit, onto exactly one node. You cannot schedule half a Pod onto one node and the other half onto another -- for scheduling purposes, the Pod is indivisible.

The overwhelming majority of Pods you'll encounter contain exactly one container, and it's tempting, in that common case, to treat 'Pod' and 'container' as basically synonymous. They're not, and the distinction matters the moment you need a second, tightly coupled helper process that must live and die alongside your main container, share its network identity, and be scheduled onto the exact same node -- a log shipper, a TLS-terminating proxy, a file synchronizer. Kubernetes' answer to 'these processes are inseparable' is the Pod: the unit that captures exactly that guarantee, so you never have to worry about the scheduler placing your app on one node and its required sidecar on another.

sections.heading: What Containers in a Pod Actually Share
sections.body:
Containers within the same Pod share a **network namespace**: they get exactly one Pod IP address between them, and exactly one shared port space. Two containers in the same Pod cannot both bind port 8080 -- attempting it fails with 'address already in use,' the same way it would for two processes on a single traditional host, precisely because as far as the network stack is concerned, that's exactly what they are. Containers in the same Pod talk to each other over `localhost`, not over the Pod's external IP, because from inside either container's network namespace, the other container's listening ports are simply local ports.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-with-sidecar
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
    - name: metrics-sidecar
      image: metrics-exporter:2.1
      ports:
        - containerPort: 9090
```

Containers can also optionally share **volumes**: storage defined once at the Pod level and mounted into any number of its containers. A common pattern is an `emptyDir` volume that one container writes to and another reads from -- purely local disk sharing on whichever node the Pod happens to land on, with no network call involved at all.

What containers in a Pod do **not** share by default is the **PID (process) namespace** -- each container keeps its own isolated process tree, so running `ps aux` inside container A will not show container B's processes, unless the Pod explicitly opts in with `shareProcessNamespace: true`. This is worth knowing precisely because it corrects the natural but wrong assumption that 'sharing a Pod' means 'sharing everything a VM would share' -- it shares specific, deliberately chosen namespaces and volumes, not the whole OS-level environment indiscriminately.

sections.heading: Init Containers vs. Main Containers
sections.body:
A Pod can declare `initContainers`, which run to completion, strictly in the order listed, before any of the Pod's regular containers start at all. If an init container fails, the kubelet restarts it according to the Pod's `restartPolicy` -- and critically, none of the regular containers will start until every init container has exited successfully. This makes init containers the natural place for genuinely sequential setup work: waiting for a dependency to become reachable, running a one-time migration, fetching a config bundle -- anything that must complete, in order, before the main application should even attempt to start.

```yaml
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
```

Regular containers, by contrast, all start at roughly the same time once init containers finish, with no ordering guarantee among themselves, and they run for the Pod's entire lifetime. When one of those regular containers exists purely to support the main workload -- a log shipper, a proxy, a cache warmer -- it's informally called a **sidecar**, even though structurally it's just another entry in the same `containers` list. (Recent Kubernetes versions add a more formal 'sidecar container' feature, letting a container in `initContainers` set `restartPolicy: Always` to get defined startup ordering plus a long running lifecycle -- but the classic pattern worth understanding first is simply: another regular, always-running container, colocated in the same Pod.)

sections.heading: Pods Are Cattle, Not Pets: Ephemerality and Identity
sections.body:
This is the single biggest mental shift coming from VM-based operations. If a container inside a Pod crashes, the kubelet restarts *that specific container*, in place, within the *same* Pod -- same name, same IP, governed by `restartPolicy`. That part does feel like rebooting a service on a VM.

But if the *Pod itself* is deleted, evicted, or lost along with its node, it is gone permanently -- there is no 'restarting the Pod' in that scenario. What you'll observe instead, assuming the Pod is managed by a controller (covered next module), is a *replacement* Pod being created fresh: a new name, and critically, a new IP address. Nothing about the replacement Pod is a revival of the old one; it's a brand-new object that merely happens to be built from the same template. You should never hardcode, cache, or build automation around a specific Pod's IP surviving anything -- that exact gap, 'the set of backing IPs changes constantly and unpredictably,' is precisely the problem Services (covered in the next module) exist to paper over.

One more detail worth internalizing here: Pods are almost never created directly in a production system. You certainly *can* run `kubectl run` and get a bare Pod, and it will work fine right up until something goes wrong -- because a bare Pod has no controller watching it, so if it's deleted or its node fails, nothing recreates it; it just stays dead. That's a direct violation of the self-healing premise from the Declarative vs. Imperative concept. In practice, Pods are almost always created indirectly, through a controller (a Deployment, a StatefulSet, a Job) that supplies exactly the reconciliation loop needed to keep the *right number* of Pods matching a template in existence, which is the entire subject of the next module.

examples.title: A Multi-Container Pod Sharing a Volume and a Network Namespace
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-with-sidecar
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: shared-logs
      emptyDir: {}
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
      volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-logs
          mountPath: /var/log/app
    - name: log-shipper
      image: log-shipper:1.2
      volumeMounts:
        - name: shared-logs
          mountPath: /var/log/app
          readOnly: true
examples.explanation: Both containers mount the same `emptyDir` volume, `shared-logs`, at the same path -- and because they're in the same Pod, scheduled together onto the same node, this is literally the same directory on that node's filesystem underneath both of them. The log-shipper container can tail files the app container writes with zero network calls involved; it's pure local-disk sharing, which only works at all because a Pod's volumes are a Pod-level construct, mounted into whichever of its containers ask for them. Separately, both containers also share exactly one network namespace and therefore one IP: if app needed to reach a metrics endpoint the log-shipper exposed on port 9090, it would curl `localhost:9090`, not the Pod's external IP -- and if app itself were also trying to bind port 9090, that would conflict, precisely because there is only one port space for the whole Pod, unlike two separate Pods, which would each get their own independent port space entirely.

examples.title: Ephemerality: A Replacement Pod Is Not the Same Pod
examples.code:
kubectl get pod web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp -o wide
# NAME                     READY   STATUS    IP            NODE
# web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp      1/1     Running   10.244.1.14   node-2

kubectl delete pod web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp
# pod "web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp" deleted

# (Deployment's ReplicaSet controller notices the count dropped and creates a replacement)
kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide
# NAME                     READY   STATUS    IP            NODE
# web-7d9f8c9b7-9plm2      1/1     Running   10.244.2.31   node-3
examples.explanation: The replacement Pod has a different generated name suffix, a different IP address (10.244.2.31 instead of 10.244.1.14), and even landed on a different node -- nothing here is the original Pod 'coming back.' It's a completely new object, created from scratch by the ReplicaSet controller because it observed the actual replica count drop below the desired count, exactly the reconciliation behavior from the previous concept. Anything that had cached or hardcoded 10.244.1.14 as 'the web Pod's address' is now silently talking to nothing. This is exactly why nothing in a healthy Kubernetes setup should ever address an individual Pod by its IP directly -- and exactly the gap a Service's stable virtual IP is designed to close, which is where the next module picks up.

misconceptions.description: A Pod is basically just Kubernetes' name for a single container -- in casual conversation 'Pod' and 'container' mean the same thing, and that's fine because in practice they usually are the same thing.
misconceptions.clarification: The common one-container-per-Pod case creates that illusion, but a Pod is a distinct scheduling and resource-sharing boundary that can hold multiple containers sharing one network namespace and, optionally, volumes. The conflation breaks down the moment you meet any sidecar pattern, or need to reason about restartPolicy (which applies at the Pod level, governing every container inside it identically) or about why two containers in the same Pod can't both bind the same port (a constraint that has nothing to do with containers in general, and everything to do with the specific Pod-level network namespace they happen to share).

misconceptions.description: If a Pod is deleted -- whether by a person, an eviction, or a node failure -- Kubernetes 'heals' it by restarting that exact same Pod object in place, preserving its identity and IP, like rebooting a VM.
misconceptions.clarification: Container-level restart and Pod-level replacement are two entirely different mechanisms. When a single container inside a Pod crashes, the kubelet does restart that container in place, within the same Pod, keeping the same IP -- that part genuinely does resemble a VM reboot. But once the Pod object itself is deleted or evicted, it is gone permanently; there is no repair-in-place operation for a whole Pod. If something is watching the count (a ReplicaSet), it reacts by creating a brand-new Pod object -- new name, new IP -- not by resurrecting the old one. Treating a Pod's IP as durable across this kind of event is a real, common source of production bugs.

exercises.prompt: This Pod defines two containers that both try to bind port 8080. What happens when the Pod is created, and why is this fundamentally different from two separate Pods each trying to bind port 8080 on the same node?
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: port-conflict
spec:
  containers:
    - name: server-a
      image: my-server:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
    - name: server-b
      image: my-other-server:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
hints: How many network namespaces does this single Pod have in total -- one shared by both containers, or one per container?
Binding a port twice within a single network namespace behaves the same way it would for two ordinary processes on one traditional host.
Think about whether Kubernetes would even reject this at apply time, or whether the failure happens later, inside one of the running containers.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Kubernetes accepts the manifest -- there's no validation against duplicate containerPort declarations. But at runtime, whichever container's process tries to bind port 8080 second will fail with an 'address already in use' error, because both containers share exactly one network namespace and therefore one port space for the whole Pod. That container will likely crash-loop. Two separate Pods each binding 8080 would have no conflict at all, because each Pod gets its own independent network namespace and IP.
exercises.solutionExplanation: containerPort in a Pod spec is documentation/metadata for humans and tooling -- it doesn't reserve the port or prevent a collision; Kubernetes does not validate that two containers in the same Pod use different ports. The actual conflict happens at the OS level, inside whichever container's process calls bind(8080) second within that shared network namespace, and fails exactly the way two ordinary processes on one host would if both tried to listen on the same port. Depending on restartPolicy, the kubelet will likely keep restarting the failing container, producing a CrashLoopBackOff. This has nothing to do with containers in isolation -- two entirely separate Pods, each with its own independent network namespace and IP, could both happily bind port 8080 with zero conflict, because 'the port space' is scoped per-Pod, not global to the node or the cluster.

exercises.prompt: This Pod is meant to wait for a database to become reachable before the app container starts, but both containers start at the same time, creating a race condition where the app sometimes fails to connect. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
hints: All entries under `containers:` start together, with no ordering guarantee between them -- is that really what should be true for a container whose entire purpose is to run and finish BEFORE anything else?
Kubernetes has a dedicated field for containers that must run to completion, strictly in order, before any regular container starts.
The fix is about which list this container belongs to, not about changing its command.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-for-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:1.0
exercises.solutionExplanation: In the original spec, wait-for-db was listed under `containers`, which means it starts at roughly the same time as app, with no guarantee it finishes -- or even starts -- before app tries to connect to the database, which is exactly the race condition described. Moving it into `initContainers` changes its behavior entirely: init containers run to completion, strictly in the order listed, and the kubelet will not start any regular container until every init container has exited successfully (exit code 0). With this fix, `app` is now guaranteed not to start until `wait-for-db`'s loop has actually detected the database is reachable and exited, eliminating the race by construction rather than by hoping the timing works out.

assessments.prompt: Two containers, A and B, are defined in the same Pod spec with no special namespace-sharing options set. Which of these is something they share by default?
options: The same PID (process) namespace, so `ps aux` inside container A shows container B's processes too.
The same network namespace, so they share one Pod IP and can reach each other over localhost.
The same root filesystem, so a file written by container A at /tmp/data.txt is automatically visible to container B at the same path.
The same container image, so both containers necessarily run identical code.
assessments.explanation: Containers in the same Pod share a network namespace by default -- one Pod IP, one port space, and localhost reachability between them -- which is precisely why two containers in one Pod can't both bind the same port. Option A is false by default: PID namespaces are isolated per container unless the Pod explicitly sets shareProcessNamespace: true. Option C is false: each container has its own independent root filesystem from its own image; only explicitly declared shared volumes (like emptyDir) are visible across containers, and only at the specific paths where each container chooses to mount them. Option D is false and conflates 'same Pod' with 'same image' -- a Pod's containers are typically built from entirely different images serving different purposes, such as an app and a sidecar.

assessments.prompt: A Pod defines two init containers, `fetch-config` and `run-migration`, listed in that order, followed by one regular container `app`. If `fetch-config` fails (a non-zero exit code) and the Pod's restartPolicy is `Always`, what happens?
options: `run-migration` and `app` start immediately anyway, since init container failures are only logged as warning events and never block anything.

The kubelet restarts `fetch-config` according to the restartPolicy; `run-migration` and `app` will not start until `fetch-config` eventually exits successfully, because init containers run strictly in the order listed and none of the regular containers start until every init container has completed successfully.
The kubelet skips `fetch-config` after one failed attempt and proceeds directly to `run-migration`, since init containers are treated as best-effort by design.
The whole Pod object is permanently deleted the moment any init container fails, forcing a controller to create an entirely new Pod.
assessments.explanation: Init containers are a strict, ordered gate: each one must exit successfully before the next init container (or, once all are done, the regular containers) is allowed to start at all. A failing init container is restarted according to the Pod's restartPolicy just like a regular container would be, but critically, nothing downstream of it -- neither run-migration nor app -- starts until it eventually succeeds. There is no best-effort skipping and no automatic whole-Pod deletion triggered purely by an init container failure; the Pod simply stays not-Ready, retrying the failed init container, until it either succeeds or the Pod's backoff/restart behavior is otherwise addressed.

assessments.prompt: A developer runs `kubectl run debug-pod --image=busybox` to get a bare Pod with no owning Deployment, ReplicaSet, or other controller. The node it lands on is later drained and removed from the cluster. What happens to debug-pod?
options: A replacement Pod is automatically created on a different node, exactly as if it had been managed by a Deployment, because the scheduler itself tracks and re-places all Pods regardless of ownership.
debug-pod is gone permanently, and nothing recreates it -- a bare Pod has no controller running a reconciliation loop that would notice its absence and act on it, so it simply stays deleted.
The kubelet on whichever node it would have been rescheduled to automatically adopts it, preserving its original name and IP.
The API server itself detects the orphaned Pod and re-creates it as a built-in safety default, independent of any controller.
assessments.explanation: Self-healing in Kubernetes isn't a property of Pods themselves -- it comes entirely from a controller's reconciliation loop noticing that the observed count no longer matches a declared desired count and acting on the gap. A bare Pod created directly has no such controller watching it, no ReplicaSet declaring 'there should be one of these,' so when it's lost along with its node, there is genuinely nothing left to notice the loss or recreate it. This is exactly why Pods are almost never created directly in production -- they're created indirectly through a Deployment, StatefulSet, or Job specifically to get this reconciliation guarantee, which a bare Pod deliberately lacks.

assessments.prompt: A single container inside a running, multi-container Pod crashes due to an unhandled exception, while the rest of the Pod is unaffected. Assuming a normal restartPolicy, what happens to the Pod's identity (its name and IP address) as a result?
options: The whole Pod is deleted and a brand-new Pod is created with a new name and new IP, since any single container's failure is treated as a failure of the entire Pod.

The kubelet restarts just that one container in place, within the same Pod object -- the Pod keeps its original name and IP throughout, unlike what happens when the Pod object itself is deleted or evicted.
The Pod's IP changes but its name stays the same, because IP addresses are reassigned to a Pod every time any of its containers restart, for security isolation.
Nothing restarts automatically at all; a human must manually delete the Pod before any controller will create a working replacement.
assessments.explanation: This is the distinction between container-level restart and Pod-level replacement: when one container inside a Pod crashes, the kubelet restarts that specific container in place, within the same Pod object, and the Pod's name and IP are completely unaffected because the Pod itself was never deleted -- only one process inside it was. Full Pod replacement, with a new name and new IP, only happens when the Pod object itself is deleted, evicted, or lost with its node, which is an entirely different scenario driven by a controller creating a fresh replacement, not by the kubelet's ordinary container-restart behavior.

assessments.prompt: Explain why a Pod, not an individual container, is the smallest unit Kubernetes actually schedules and manages, and describe specifically what would break if Kubernetes instead scheduled and scaled containers independently of one another.
assessments.modelAnswer: Kubernetes schedules Pods because some units of deployable work genuinely need more than one container acting as a single, inseparable thing -- most commonly a main application container plus a tightly coupled helper like a log shipper or a proxy sidecar, both of which need to be colocated on the same node, share a network identity, and rise and fall together as one unit. The Pod is the abstraction that captures exactly that requirement: it's the boundary the scheduler treats as atomic (never splitting a Pod's containers across two nodes), the boundary that defines one shared network namespace and IP (letting sidecars talk to the main container over localhost with no network hop), and the boundary that defines shared, optional volumes for local, no-network data exchange between containers. If Kubernetes instead scheduled and scaled individual containers independently, several things would immediately break: a sidecar could end up placed on a completely different node from the main container it's meant to support, defeating the entire point of colocated helpers; there would be no natural mechanism for giving a pair of tightly coupled containers a single shared IP and localhost reachability, since each container would need its own independent network identity; and scaling would become incoherent -- if 'scale to 3' meant three independent containers rather than three copies of a coupled group, there would be no guarantee you'd end up with matched app-and-sidecar pairs at all, only however many of each happened to be scheduled. The Pod exists specifically to make 'these containers are inseparable, so treat them as one atomic unit for scheduling, networking, and lifecycle' a first-class, explicit concept, rather than something every user has to hand-roll with ad hoc coordination.
